routes.description: Establish that naturally developed, reasons-responsive self-control constitutes the freedom relevant to moral agency and can support ordinary desert, responsibility, sanctions, and reactive practices without requiring ultimate self-creation or indeterminism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects practical control and moral competence to meaningful alternatives, distinguishes ordinary causation from responsibility-undermining interference, and explains why stable responsibility practices and proportionate consequences remain justified under determinism.

motionBridge.description: Show that natural reasons-responsive control is sufficient to justify compatibilist freedom, ordinary desert, and responsibility practices.

centralBridges.description: Define the relevant freedom through informed, unimpaired, reasons-responsive self-control rather than randomness or ultimate metaphysical authorship.
Explain how learning, reflection, practice, and moral education make agents sufficiently autonomous and accountable despite deterministic causal histories.
Justify proportionate, public, rule-governed sanctions and blame as components of a secure cooperative social order.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish deliberate interpersonal control from impersonal causal determination in assessing whether an agent's control has been displaced.
Account for morally condemnatory reactions as fitting and behavior-guiding responses to serious wrongdoing by competent adults.

routes.description: Establish that reasons-responsive agency does not supply the ultimate control required for basic desert, while showing that protection, deterrence, rehabilitation, moral engagement, and rule enforcement remain available on forward-looking grounds.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it separates practical agency from basic-desert responsibility, shows why neither determinism nor indeterminism supplies ultimate control, and provides non-desert foundations for justified social responses without retaining retribution or desert-dependent anger.

motionBridge.description: Show that natural reasons-responsive control does not justify basic desert and that defensible responsibility practices need not presuppose it.

centralBridges.description: Argue that agents are not ultimate sources of their characters and actions under either deterministic or indeterministic causal conditions.
Show that reasons-responsiveness and compatibilist agent control can matter practically without establishing desert-based blame or punishment.
Ground coercion, deterrence, rehabilitation, and rule enforcement in public safety, future risk, proportionality, and least-restrictive means.
Require an independent role for backward-looking desert beyond what consequentialist institutions and causal responsibility already provide.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use manipulation and malfunction cases to test whether internal psychological responsiveness is sufficient for responsibility.
Explain how evolved reactive attitudes and responsibility practices can be revised without surrendering their protective or communicative functions.

sections.title: Reasons-Responsive Control and the Ability to Do Otherwise
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether informed, unimpaired responsiveness to reasons constitutes the relevant practical control and meaningful alternative possibilities, or whether those capacities fall short of the freedom needed for desert.

sections.title: Sourcehood, Determinism, and Manipulation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether deterministic histories undermine accountable agency, whether developed self-control supplies adequate sourcehood, and whether manipulation cases reveal a relevant gap between causation and control.

sections.title: Basic Desert and Ordinary Compatibilist Desert
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the central conceptual dispute over whether basic desert is required, whether ordinary conduct-sensitive desert is independently defensible, and whether reasons-responsive agency can bridge the two notions.

sections.title: Punishment, Public Safety, and Institutional Justification
sections.rationale: This issue compares rule-governed punishment and proportional sanctions with quarantine, deterrence, rehabilitation, and least-restrictive protection as foundations for legitimate coercive practices.

sections.title: Reactive Attitudes and Reform of Responsibility Practices
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether moral anger and condemnation are justified or indispensable, and whether evolved practices can instead be revised toward non-desert attitudes while retaining social regulation and moral communication.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Introducing indeterminacy into deliberation does not provide desert-grounding control because the agent still cannot settle which of the supported outcomes occurs.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker distinguishes recent libertarian accounts and evaluates their strategically placed indeterminacy before concluding that agents lack the required control.

response.rationale: This is a constructive argument against indeterminacy as a source of ultimate control, so it has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states a focused objection and the relevant settlement gap.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable and expressly limited to libertarian accounts that introduce indeterminacy without agent settlement.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion tracks the stated inability of indeterminacy alone to explain which supported outcome occurs.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unsettled outcomes to failure of desert-grounding control is clear, with only the desert criterion compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual settlement argument is directly stated, though rival agent-causal mechanisms are not examined in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central ultimate-control bridge but does not by itself complete the broader skeptical route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The excerpt attacks a specified model but does not meaningfully compare a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes libertarian types and identifies the agent's inability to settle which indeterminate outcome occurs.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Because who agents are and what they do ultimately result from factors beyond their control, basic-desert responsibility is absent under either determinism or indeterminism.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso explicitly identifies himself as the free-will skeptic, contrasts Dennett as the compatibilist, and states the defining thesis of his position.

response.rationale: This is a constructive statement of the skeptical route's central sourcehood thesis and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the position, causal premise, and specifically limited responsibility conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly limits the denial to a particular pervasive basic-desert sense of moral responsibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical conclusion exceeds the brief support supplied for the move from uncontrolled factors to absent basic desert.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The sourcehood premise connects coherently to basic-desert denial, but the required ultimate-control principle remains implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt asserts that agents ultimately result from uncontrolled factors without defending that sweeping causal premise here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly states the motion-level skeptical thesis linking natural agency to the absence of basic-desert responsibility.

representationalCharity.rationale: This passage states the speaker's own thesis without developing or characterizing a competing account.

moves.evidenceBasis: Caruso defines skepticism through factors beyond agents' control and explicitly limits the resulting denial to basic-desert responsibility.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Determinism does not eliminate the responsibility-relevant ability to do otherwise because people remain capable of responding to persuasion, changing their conduct, and developing moral competence.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett affirms the host's formulation and then explains a nonmetaphysical sense of alternatives through behavioral change, legal responsibility, and developing competence.

components.text: Whether agents are ultimate sources of who they are and what they do
Whether indeterminacy enables an agent to settle which supported outcome occurs

response.rationale: Practical changeability rebuts fatalistic implications of determinism, but it does not answer the earlier demand for ultimate sourcehood or outcome settlement.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a relevant nonanswer: it advances practical control while leaving the decisive ultimate-sourcehood demand untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: Practical change is clear, but its scope as an ability to do otherwise under identical conditions remains only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Observed behavioral change supports practical flexibility, but the rhetoric overstates what it establishes about responsibility-relevant alternatives.

charity.alternative: Determinism allows conduct to change across changed reasons and circumstances while still excluding ultimate sourcehood.
charity.decisiveQualification: Practical changeability alone does not establish the basic-desert control challenged by the opponent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The anti-fatalist inference is sound, but the bridge from changeability across circumstances to responsibility-relevant alternatives is underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Common observation that people change supports plasticity, while the metaphysical and responsibility bridge receives little independent support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion bridge by presenting practical changeability as responsibility-relevant control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly rejects fatalism, though it does not fully preserve the opponent's distinct ultimate-control qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dennett points to persuasion, changed lives, developing competence, and observed behavioral change despite determinism.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Free-will skepticism rejects basic-desert responsibility while preserving causal and attributive responsibility and forward-looking moral engagement grounded in reconciliation, safety, and moral formation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly yields to Gregg, and the uninterrupted first-person explanation states the skeptical position associated with his work.

components.text: Whether practical change and reasons-responsiveness justify the responsibility practices at issue

response.rationale: The move preserves practical agency but justifies replacing a general responsibility demand with the narrower basic-desert question and forward-looking alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly preserves causal and attributive responsibility while explaining the narrower disputed target and its replacement grounds.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between rejected basic desert and preserved causal, attributive, and forward-looking responsibility is explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The bounded claim that non-desert responsibility practices remain available is proportionate to the enumerated grounds.

charity.alternative: Compatibilist practical control may justify ordinary responsibility without purporting to establish ultimate self-creation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The skeptical rejection is expressly limited to basic-desert responsibility rather than all agency or accountability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinctions and forward-looking replacement are coherent, with only the full institutional derivation deferred.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Three specific forward-looking grounds are supplied, though their sufficiency for every responsibility practice is not fully defended here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the skeptical motion bridge by separating natural control from basic desert while preserving practices.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately preserves substantial compatibilist functions while isolating the narrower point of disagreement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects basic desert while grounding retained responsibility in reconciliation, future safety, and moral formation.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Basic moral desert is a misleading requirement, while sufficient ordinary moral responsibility can still justify coercion, imprisonment, fines, and reputational consequences for violations.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso directly invites Dan to respond, after which Dennett rejects basic desert and develops the Donald Trump coercion example in his characteristic first person.

components.text: Whether responsibility practices can be justified once basic-desert responsibility is rejected
Whether absence of ultimate sourcehood excludes every sufficient form of moral responsibility

response.rationale: The reply accepts that basic desert is unnecessary and directly asserts sufficient ordinary responsibility for familiar coercive consequences.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive practical implication, though the criterion making ordinary responsibility sufficient remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The consequences and limited target are clear, but 'enough moral responsibility' lacks a fully stable criterion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical authorization of imprisonment is stronger than the brief appeal to legal violations and ordinary responsibility warrants.

charity.alternative: The skeptic permits coercion but grounds it in protection rather than backward-looking desert.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing permissible coercion does not alone establish that ordinary desert performs independent justificatory work.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion follows only if ordinary responsibility independently justifies the listed sanctions, a material bridge left largely asserted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Donald Trump and law-violation example illustrates the intuition but does not defend the governing criterion or proportionality.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the motion bridge by claiming ordinary responsibility is sufficient for consequential responsibility practices.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes permissible coercion but substantially compresses the opponent's alternative non-desert justification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dennett rejects basic desert as necessary and invokes law violations and sufficient ordinary responsibility to justify coercive consequences.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Coercion and liberty restriction can be justified through self-defense, public safety, proportionality, and least-restrictive means without invoking free will, retribution, or basic desert.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn answers Dennett's challenge in the first person and develops Caruso's recognizable public-health quarantine model and least-restriction principle.

components.text: Whether justified coercion and imprisonment require ordinary moral desert
Whether retained practical agency must ground coercive responsibility practices

response.rationale: The reply directly supplies non-desert grounds for coercion and adds proportionality and least-restrictive limitations to the alternative framework.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly answers the coercion challenge with a structured alternative justification and relevant limiting principles.

precisionFindings.rationale: Public danger, self-defense, proportionality, and least-restrictive means clearly delimit the proposed coercive authority.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is carefully conditioned on significant threats, proportionality, and prevention of harm to others.

charity.alternative: The state may regard deserved consequences as part of a stable lawful response to responsible violations.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must show coercion is independently justified without claiming that no desert-based account is conceivable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy and limiting principles form a clear route from serious threats to justified preventive restrictions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The self-defense and quarantine analogy supplies a concrete warrant, though differences between disease and culpable crime remain bounded gaps.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly completes a major part of the skeptical motion bridge by grounding responsibility practices without desert.

representationalCharity.rationale: It answers the strongest practical challenge through an independent basis without caricaturing all compatibilist institutions.

moves.evidenceBasis: Caruso expressly invokes significant public danger, self-defense, harm prevention, proportionality, and least-restrictive intervention.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Deterministic causation does not eliminate accountable sourcehood because autonomous agents become largely self-made through sustained learning, reflection, practice, exposure to reasons, and moral education.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett directly addresses Gregg by name, diagnoses a confusion between causation and control, and answers the Maya and Marina thought experiment.

components.text: Whether deterministic causal histories exclude accountable sourcehood
Whether learned moral competence supports more than causal or attributive responsibility

response.rationale: The reply directly replaces ultimate self-creation with developed autonomy through learning, reflection, reasons, and moral education.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the sourcehood premise but leaves the final bridge from developed self-control to desert partly implicit.

precisionFindings.rationale: The developmental mechanisms and impaired-agent exception are explicit, though 'largely self-made' remains somewhat elastic.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The qualified claim of being largely rather than ultimately self-made fits the developmental considerations offered.

charity.alternative: A person may develop through reasons while the capacities and history enabling that development remain ultimately uncontrolled.
charity.decisiveQualification: Developed autonomy answers practical sourcehood but does not itself refute the skeptic's ultimate-source requirement.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Development plausibly supports autonomous self-control, but its sufficiency for desert rather than competence is an implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Learning, practice, reflection, reasons, and moral education provide concrete support, with no detailed rival-case comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central development bridge by explaining autonomy as an acquired capacity under determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the strongest causal concern fairly, while the remaining difference over ultimate sourcehood is compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dennett cites twenty years of learning, practice, reflection, exposure to reasons, and moral education, while recognizing defective self-control.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: An undamaged, informed, reasons-responsive, and self-controlled person can meaningfully be said to have been able to do otherwise despite deterministic causation.
moves.attributionBasis: Following the question about alternative possibilities, Dennett gives a first-person clarification centered on degrees of freedom, self-control, and reasons-responsive functioning.

components.text: Whether deterministic causation rules out a meaningful responsibility-relevant alternative ability
Whether alternative ability must consist in settling an indeterminate outcome

response.rationale: The reply offers a compatibilist criterion of alternative ability based on freedom from impairment, misinformation, restraint, and defective reasons-responsiveness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supplies the disputed alternative criterion, although it does not fully argue why that criterion answers basic desert.

precisionFindings.rationale: The operative ability is defined through explicit conditions of information, freedom from restraint, reasons, and functioning.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stipulated compatibilist meaning, the asserted ability is matched to the explicit unimpaired-function conditions.

charity.alternative: The skeptic can accept conditional practical ability while denying categorical alternatives or basic-desert control.
charity.decisiveQualification: The proposed criterion establishes ordinary functional freedom, not automatically the opponent's ultimate-control standard.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The criterion is internally coherent and concretely specified, with one remaining normative bridge to desert.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The listed impairment contrasts support the functional criterion, but its superiority to rival readings is not fully defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central control bridge by defining the responsibility-relevant ability in compatibilist terms.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly states an alternative concept of ability, though it does not fully engage the skeptic's distinct desert qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines ability otherwise through degrees of freedom, self-control, adequate information, reasons, and normal functioning.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Compatibilist agent control and freedom from intentional external manipulation are distinct, and possessing reasons-responsive control leaves open whether basic-desert responsibility is justified.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso announces a return to Dennett's causation-control distinction and develops the two loci of control before stating the unresolved sufficiency challenge.

components.text: Whether developed reasons-responsive self-control is sufficient for desert-based responsibility
Whether an unimpaired compatibilist ability otherwise supplies desert-grounding control
Whether practical changeability resolves the separate sufficiency question about desert

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses an equivocation between agent control and freedom from interpersonal control, then states that desert sufficiency remains unestablished.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the inference gap and states the defeating consequence for the compatibilist sufficiency claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two loci of control and the residual question concerning desert-based responsibility are expressly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move carefully claims an open sufficiency question rather than claiming that reasons-responsive control has been disproved.

charity.alternative: Compatibilist control may be sufficient because responsibility concerns an agent's functioning rather than ultimate authorship.
charity.decisiveQualification: Freedom from intentional interference and internal agent control are distinct, and neither alone settles basic desert.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction directly undercuts the inference from possessed control to desert, and the limited conclusion is well matched.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several recognized argument types are identified as reasons the question remains open, though they are not developed in this excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central sufficiency-gap bridge by separating practical agent control from desert justification.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move grants the compatibilist form of control and accurately isolates the remaining normative sufficiency dispute.

moves.evidenceBasis: Caruso distinguishes internal agent control from freedom from intentional external control and lists multiple unresolved skeptical arguments.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Deliberate control by other agents differs responsibility-relevantly from impersonal natural causation because social institutions must address planned interpersonal interference that displaces another person's control.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett directly denies the question-begging charge and explains the social significance of control by other agents.

components.text: Whether interpersonal manipulation differs responsibility-relevantly from ordinary natural causation
Whether all uncontrolled causal antecedents are equivalent to another agent displacing control

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes planned interpersonal interference from impersonal causation by its institutional and control-displacing significance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the manipulation distinction clearly but only indirectly addresses whether the distinction establishes basic desert.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly limited to other agents' planned projects that interfere with another person's control.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The institutional distinction is supported by the specified social role of intentional, planned interference.

charity.alternative: Manipulation cases may reveal that internally reasons-responsive mechanisms can still originate in responsibility-undermining histories.
charity.decisiveQualification: Political importance of interpersonal interference does not alone establish that causal history is irrelevant to desert.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The institutional distinction is coherent, though its inference to individual desert rather than social regulation is incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Planned social interference provides a concrete distinguishing feature, but difficult manipulation analogies receive no extended comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary manipulation bridge by identifying why interpersonal control differs from natural causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes displaced control but partly shifts from the skeptic's sufficiency test to institutional significance.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dennett appeals to laws, social agents, deliberate plans, and projects that interfere with another agent's activities and control.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: A forward-looking public-health model can preserve distinctions among intentional, accidental, and habitually negligent conduct by tracking future danger and the protection each case warrants.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso gives the extended answer, identifies his model, and uses three parent cases to explain differing interventions and responsibility concepts.

components.text: Whether a forward-looking system can preserve distinctions involving intention and control
Whether legal distinctions and interventions require desert-based moral responsibility

response.rationale: The reply explains how intentional, accidental, and negligent cases generate different future risks and therefore different warranted interventions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the institutional-distinction challenge with several differentiated cases and an explicit decision variable.

precisionFindings.rationale: The model's criterion is explicitly future danger, and its application is differentiated across specified conduct types.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The bounded claim that the model can preserve distinctions is proportionate to the supplied comparative examples.

charity.alternative: Intentional and negligent distinctions may track deserved blame rather than only predicted future danger.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move need only show that non-desert risk variables can preserve legally important distinctions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Different future risks coherently support different interventions, though exact risk assessment and proportionality rules remain compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The three-parent comparison provides specific representative support, with empirical prediction reliability left undeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central alternative-practices bridge by explaining differentiated intervention without desert.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply squarely handles the functional challenge while leaving open the opponent's separate interpretation of those distinctions.

moves.evidenceBasis: Caruso uses intentional, accidental, and negligent parental cases to link conduct patterns with different future threats and protections.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Determinism and free-will skepticism preserve rational deliberation, persuasion, belief revision, and reasons-responsive action because reasons can remain causally effective.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso labels the objection a recurring misconception and answers it by aligning his view with compatibilists on deliberation and reasons as causes.

components.text: Whether skepticism and determinism undermine deliberation, persuasion, or behavioral change
Whether reasons-responsive functioning remains possible without desert-grounding freedom

response.rationale: The reply agrees that reasons cause belief and action changes while denying that this shared practical agency resolves the desert dispute.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the anti-fatalism point and preserves its force within a skeptical account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The preserved capacities are specifically enumerated and distinguished from the disputed basic-desert freedom.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The common-ground assertion that deterministic reasons can causally affect beliefs and actions fits the stated mechanism.

charity.alternative: Compatibilists infer freedom from the same reasons-responsive deliberative capacities the skeptic preserves.
charity.decisiveQualification: Agreement about rational efficacy does not establish agreement about the desert consequences of that efficacy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility of deterministic causation with reasons as causes is stated clearly and avoids the fatalistic inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Belief revision and action change supply a concrete causal explanation, though empirical documentation is not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central sufficiency-gap bridge by preserving reasons-responsiveness without conceding desert.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fully grants the practical compatibilist insight and accurately locates the remaining disagreement.

moves.evidenceBasis: Caruso expressly agrees that rational deliberation survives determinism and explains that reasons change beliefs which cause actions.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Public and proportionate punishment can sustain respect for law and instantiate a consequentialist notion of desert whose justification does not depend on whether determinism is true.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett receives the floor by name and presents a continuous account of law, punishment, desert, and exceptions for impaired agents.

components.text: Whether public safety and legitimate coercion require abandoning desert language and punishment
Whether public institutions can maintain law, proportionality, and impaired-agent exceptions
Whether consequential institutions remain justified independently of determinism

response.rationale: The reply offers public, proportionate, consequentially justified punishment and exceptions for impaired agents as an institutional alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly defends punishment's forward-looking institutional role, though the independent role of desert remains underexplained.

precisionFindings.rationale: 'Consequentialist desert' is somewhat unstable, but publicity, proportionality, law, and impairment exceptions constrain the claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion that law systems are obviously worth preserving exceeds the excerpt's limited comparison with nonpunitive alternatives.

charity.alternative: Public safety, deterrence, and legal order may be sustained without calling imposed consequences deserved punishment.
charity.decisiveQualification: The defense must identify what desert adds beyond the acknowledged good consequences of stable rules.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Consequences coherently support stable legal sanctions, but labeling the resulting account desert-based adds an insufficiently explained step.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Law, proportionality, publicity, and impairment exceptions are specific supports, while comparative institutional evidence is absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion bridge by connecting responsibility, desert, and proportionate public practices under determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move addresses institutional necessity but gives limited attention to the strongest non-desert functional equivalent.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dennett grounds law and punishment in good consequences, respect for rules, proportionality, publicity, and exceptions for impairment.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Basic moral desert posits a nonexistent requirement, whereas the desert that matters is the familiar, conduct-sensitive everyday notion and is compatible with deterministic causation.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett is explicitly invited to reply and contrasts basic moral desert with ordinary practices of deserving outcomes, rewards, and punishment.

components.text: Whether the relevant ordinary notion of desert requires ultimate sourcehood or basic desert
Whether rejecting basic desert also requires abandoning familiar conduct-sensitive deservingness
Whether deterministic reasons-responsive agency can support ordinary desert

response.rationale: The reply rejects basic desert as empty and identifies familiar conduct-sensitive deservingness as the relevant compatibilist alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the conceptual target directly, though familiar usage alone does not establish the alternative's justificatory sufficiency.

precisionFindings.rationale: Basic and everyday desert are distinguished, but the exact normative content of everyday desert remains partly unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling basic desert a term for nothing and treating familiarity as sufficient substantially exceeds the argument supplied.

charity.alternative: Basic desert is a substantive claim about blameworthiness independent of future benefits, not merely unfamiliar vocabulary.
charity.decisiveQualification: Everyday conduct-sensitive usage may be coherent while failing to justify punishment or hostile blame.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conceptual distinction is usable, but the inference from familiar everyday usage to morally justificatory desert is substantial and unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The better-team example documents ordinary language but provides weak support for desert-based blame or coercive consequences.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the motion-level dispute by defending an ordinary deterministic conception of desert.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the competing category but materially weakens it by dismissing basic desert as empty without argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dennett contrasts basic desert with familiar deservingness and illustrates everyday usage through a better-team example.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Because responsibility practices are socially evolved and historically changeable, society can further reform them by relinquishing harmful notions of just desert and retribution.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage occurs within Caruso's clearly marked response turn and presents his characteristic reformist argument against basic-desert practices.

components.text: Whether familiar and socially embedded desert practices are fixed or normatively indispensable
Whether evolved legal and responsibility practices can be further revised

response.rationale: The reply uses prior cultural change to argue that present desert and retributive practices are revisable rather than indispensable.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the appeal to familiarity, although historical revisability alone does not prove the proposed reform is superior.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is framed as hope for further reform and identifies the specific concepts proposed for relinquishment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest possibility claim is proportionate to the historical observation that responsibility cultures have changed.

charity.alternative: Evolved desert practices may be revisable yet retain valuable functions that replacement practices cannot duplicate.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical change establishes possibility of reform, not the dispensability or harmfulness of every desert concept.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Past cultural change supports possible further reform, while the transition from possibility to desirability remains appropriately qualified.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The honor-culture comparison supplies a concrete example, but harm and replacement-effectiveness claims remain lightly supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary reform bridge by establishing that reactive and responsibility practices can change.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move makes the limited revisability inference fairly and avoids claiming that historical change alone proves success.

moves.evidenceBasis: Caruso invokes the historical movement from honor cultures to individualistic cultures as evidence that responsibility practices can evolve.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: If backward-looking desert performs genuine justificatory work in a punishment theory, that theory is mixed rather than purely consequentialist; if desert performs none, it should be removed.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso resumes the conceptual challenge in an extended turn, contrasting his forward-looking conversational model with Dennett's retained backward-looking element.

components.text: Whether consequentialist desert performs independent justificatory work in punishment
Whether familiar backward-looking desert adds justification beyond forward-looking consequences

response.rationale: The reply identifies a dilemma: justificatory desert makes the theory mixed, while nonjustificatory desert is dispensable, undermining the claimed purely consequentialist position.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly targets the opponent's classification, states both branches, and gives the defeating consequence for each.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two exhaustive roles considered for desert are clearly stated and tied to distinct classificatory consequences.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stipulated distinction between doing justificatory work and doing none, the conditional dilemma is proportionate.

charity.alternative: Desert may be a rule-internal concept generated and justified by consequentialist institutional design.
charity.decisiveQualification: A derivative rule-level role could be consequentialist while still requiring explanation of what desert adds to rule application.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dilemma is clear and forceful, with one bounded gap concerning derivative or constitutive consequentialist roles for desert.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The opponent's expressed consequentialist desert supplies the relevant premise, though comparison with sophisticated rule-consequentialist accounts is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central desert-dispensability bridge by demanding an independent justificatory role for retained desert.

representationalCharity.rationale: The dilemma addresses the strongest ordinary reading, though a derivative rule-concept alternative is not fully developed.

moves.evidenceBasis: Caruso expressly contrasts desert that performs justificatory work with desert that can drop out of a purely consequentialist theory.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Consequentialist reasons can justify a rule-governed punishment system even though individual adjudication properly applies agreed rules rather than recalculating the consequences of punishment in each case.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly recalls a disagreement from the book and develops his familiar game and referee analogy in direct response to Caruso.

components.text: Whether rule-governed punishment can remain consequentialist when adjudicators apply rules nonconsequentially
Whether individualized forward-looking calculation should control each coercive decision
Whether stable rules can govern differentiated legal judgments

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes consequentialist system justification from rule-bound adjudication and explains why case-by-case recalculation would undermine law.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Desert-dependent moral anger can be replaced by attitudes such as disappointment or sorrow while retaining, and potentially improving, the practical work of interpersonal responsibility practices.
moves.attributionBasis: This uninterrupted first-person argument continues Caruso's identified turn and develops his established skeptical position on reactive attitudes.

components.text: Whether desert-dependent attitudes are needed for responsibility practices to perform their social functions
Whether ordinary desert reactions can be replaced without losing moral communication

response.rationale: The reply proposes disappointment and sorrow as non-desert replacements that can retain or improve interpersonal guidance and communication.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts functional indispensability, though its comparative effectiveness claim receives only an illustrative example.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim identifies the attitudes to replace, their proposed substitutes, and the limited interpersonal function at issue.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Replacement plausibility is supported, but saying it does exactly the same work and may improve outcomes exceeds the single example.

charity.alternative: Moral anger may communicate the gravity of adult wrongdoing in ways disappointment and sorrow cannot duplicate.
charity.decisiveQualification: The replacement claim must preserve condemnation and deterrent communication, not merely parental behavior correction.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Non-desert attitudes could coherently perform guiding functions, but equivalence across all reactive practices remains an implicit generalization.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The daughter example makes the proposal intelligible, while equal or greater effectiveness remains substantially unsupported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary reform bridge by proposing concrete non-desert replacements for moral anger.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move addresses functional replacement but uses a child-focused example that incompletely captures serious adult wrongdoing.

moves.evidenceBasis: Caruso proposes disappointment and sorrow in place of moral anger and claims they can perform the same interpersonal work.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Although disappointment may appropriately guide children, serious wrongdoing by competent adults can justify moral anger that also warns others against comparable misconduct.
moves.attributionBasis: The preceding handoff names Daniel Dennett, and the ensuing final comment directly answers Caruso's daughter and replacement-attitude examples.

components.text: Whether disappointment or sorrow adequately replaces moral anger for serious competent-adult wrongdoing
Whether reform should relinquish morally condemnatory anger in adult cases

response.rationale: The reply accepts disappointment for children but directly denies its adequacy for grave adult wrongdoing and asserts a warning function for anger.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the strongest replacement example and supplies an adult-wrongdoing distinction, though the justification is mostly intuitive.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is clearly limited to terrible wrongdoing by competent adults and contrasts it with guidance of younger children.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical entitlement and justification for anger rest mainly on an intuitive Trump example rather than a defended fittingness standard.

charity.alternative: Non-desert disappointment, sorrow, protest, and firm sanctions may condemn adult wrongdoing without hostile moral anger.
charity.decisiveQualification: The opponent claims functional replacement, not mildness or absence of serious public condemnation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The child-adult distinction is relevant, but the move from seriousness to justified moral anger requires a missing fittingness bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Trump illustration evokes a strong intuition but supplies little comparative evidence that anger is necessary or more effective.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary reactive-attitudes bridge by defending moral anger for competent adult wrongdoing.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply treats disappointment as inadequate but does not address stronger non-angry protest or the claim of equivalent condemnation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dennett contrasts parental disappointment with terrible adult wrongdoing and uses Donald Trump to illustrate the asserted inadequacy of disappointment.
